newsitem.title: FRANCE: Security forces in offensive against Algeria rebels.
newsitem.headline: Security forces in offensive against Algeria rebels.

text.p: Algerian security forces mounted an offensive south of Algiers and other operations in the capital after Moslem rebels posted warnings of a new bombing campaign, residents said on Thursday.
"It's a big operation near Blida. We could hear the sound of heavy gunfire from here yesterday afternoon," one resident said, speaking by telephone from Algiers.
There was no official word on the security activities.
Blida, 50 km (30 miles) south of Algiers, is the headquarters of the military region and a known bastion of Moslem fundamentalists.

Residents said Algeria's most ruthless rebel movement, the Armed Islamic Group (GIA), this week posted tracts on walls in the Casbah, the old heart of Algiers, saying they would resume bomb attacks in the city and other areas.
"They managed to put the notices up on walls even while the security forces were carrying out a search operation in the Casbah," said a resident.
"The notices didn't stay up long but it seems like they've already started carrying out their threat," he added, referring to bomb attacks in the Algiers suburb of Kouba last Monday.

Algerian newspapers on Tuesday said a series of bombings that day killed at least 18 people and wounded scores. The bombs ended a lull since a campaign in the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan that ended early in February.

On Thursday, the newspaper Le Matin said Algerian security forces had blown up a villa in the Algiers suburb of Birkhamed used for making bombs, including those in the Kouba attacks. It gave no details of casualties but around a dozen rebels were believed to have been in the house.
Earlier this week, residents said security forces killed at least 10 rebels in the Casbah during a 12-hour siege after three policemen were shot dead.
Liberte newspaper on Thursday said security forces killed five "terrorists" in a sweep near the town of Tiaret, some 240 km (150 miles) southwest of Algiers.
About 60,000 people have died in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a huge lead.
The oil and gas producing North African country, which has been without an elected parliament for the past five years, is gearing up for parliamentary elections on June 5.
